value.overview: The Dusky Antbird (Cercomacroides tyrannina) is a small, secretive insect-eating songbird of the tropical Americas. It belongs to the typical antbird family, Thamnophilidae, and usually stays in dense vegetation near the forest floor. Pairs defend year-round territories and are more often detected by their sharp calls and repeated songs than by sight. The species tolerates some secondary growth when dense understorey remains connected to taller forest.
value.classification: The Dusky Antbird is a passerine in the family Thamnophilidae. It was formerly widely treated under the genus Cercomacra; the currently used scientific name is Cercomacroides tyrannina.
value.identification: This antbird is about 14–15 cm long, with a relatively long tail and a dark, compact body. Adult males are mainly dark slate-gray, with a blackish throat and subtle white spots or patches in the wings. Females are distinctly different, with olive-brown upperparts and warm rufous or cinnamon underparts. Both sexes have a dark bill, short rounded wings, and a habit of moving through tangled vegetation in short hops and fluttering flights.
value.rangeHabitat: The Dusky Antbird ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and southward into northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring in suitable humid forest from the lowlands into the lower foothills, including areas on both Caribbean and Pacific drainage regions. It favors evergreen forest edges, streamside vegetation, clearings, and dense second growth bordering taller forest. It is usually found below about 1,200 m in Central America, though it can occur higher locally.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally sedentary throughout its range; regular seasonal migration is not known.
value.breeding: Breeding information varies geographically. In Costa Rica and Panama, breeding activity has been reported mainly from February through October, overlapping much of the wet season. The nest is a small pouch or rounded woven structure made from materials such as dead leaves, palm strips, grasses, fern stems, and fungal fibres, usually placed low in dense vegetation. The usual clutch is two eggs, which are pale and marked with reddish-brown or darker blotches.
value.dietFeeding: The Dusky Antbird feeds mainly on insects, spiders, and other small arthropods. It forages alone, in pairs, or in family groups, usually within about 5 m of the ground. Birds hop through vines, shrubs, leaf litter, and tangled understorey, taking prey by gleaning from leaves and stems, reaching or lunging from perches, and making short fluttering flights. It may occasionally attend army-ant swarms but is not an obligate ant follower.
value.behavior: This species is secretive and strongly associated with dense understorey. Pairs commonly remain within and defend a territory throughout the year, often responding to each other with coordinated songs and calls. It spends much of its time moving quietly through shaded vegetation and rarely perches in exposed locations. The Dusky Antbird only occasionally joins mixed-species feeding flocks. Its repeated vocalizations are often the best way to locate it in Costa Rican forests.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered stable, although the total population size has not been reliably quantified.
